questions.stem: In Ansoff's Matrix, selling a new product to existing customers is:
questions.why: New product, existing market. You know the customers; the product is new. Moderate risk.
whyNot: Market development is an EXISTING product to NEW customers. Students reverse these constantly.
Penetration is an existing product in an existing market.
Diversification is a new product in a new market.

questions.stem: In Ansoff's Matrix, selling an existing product in a new country is:
questions.why: Existing product, new market. The product is familiar; the customers, culture and regulations are not.
whyNot: Product development would mean creating a new product.
Penetration means the same product to the same market.
Diversification requires both to be new.

questions.stem: Which Ansoff strategy carries the highest risk?
questions.why: New product in a new market means nothing is familiar. Its attraction is that it spreads risk away from dependence on one market.
whyNot: Penetration is the lowest risk, because both product and market are known.
Moderate risk: the market is known.
Moderate risk: the product is known.

questions.stem: Which Ansoff strategy is limited by market saturation?
questions.why: Selling more of the same thing to the same market works until the market is full. Then growth requires moving to another box.
whyNot: Diversification enters an entirely new market, so saturation of the old one is not the constraint.
Market development moves into new markets specifically to escape saturation.
A new product creates new demand in the same market.

questions.stem: In Porter's Strategic Matrix, what are the two dimensions?
options: Basis of advantage (cost or differentiation) and scope (broad or narrow)
questions.why: Porter asks whether you compete on being cheapest or being different, and whether you do it across a broad market or a narrow segment.
whyNot: Those are Ansoff's dimensions.
Those are the Boston Matrix dimensions.
Not a Porter framework.

questions.stem: What does Porter mean by being stuck in the middle?
options: The business is neither clearly cheapest nor clearly different, so customers have no reason to choose it
The business is in the middle of its market in terms of size
The business has a moderate market share
The business operates in several countries
questions.why: It cannot win on price against the cost leader or on quality against the differentiator. Porter argues you must choose one.
whyNot: Size is not what the matrix measures.
Share is not a Porter dimension.
Geography is unrelated to the matrix.

questions.stem: What is the main criticism of Porter's stuck in the middle argument?
options: Some businesses have combined efficient low-cost operations with a strong brand successfully
Porter's matrix has only three boxes
Cost leadership is impossible to achieve
questions.why: Because there are real counterexamples, treat it as a warning rather than a law, and say so. That nuance is worth an evaluation mark.
whyNot: It has four cells.
Cost leadership is a well-established strategy.
Differentiation succeeds routinely.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strategic rather than a tactical decision?
questions.why: Strategic decisions are long term, high risk, taken at senior level and difficult to reverse. The others are short term and easily changed.
whyNot: Short term, low risk, easily reversed.
A routine operational decision.
A day-to-day management decision.

questions.stem: Why are strategic decisions difficult to reverse?
options: They commit large sums to assets and capabilities that cannot easily be sold or unlearned
The law prevents businesses from changing strategy
Senior managers are not allowed to change their minds
questions.why: Money spent on premises, equipment, training and market entry is largely sunk. That is why the cost of being wrong on a strategic decision is so high.
whyNot: No legal restriction exists.
They can, and the resources already committed are the problem.
Many strategic decisions fail.

questions.stem: Why should a small guesthouse operator usually pursue market penetration before diversification?
options: Risk rises with distance from what the business already knows, and its finance is limited
Diversification is illegal for small businesses
questions.why: Penetration uses existing knowledge of both product and market, so the risk and the cash requirement are lowest. A small operator cannot absorb the failure of a diversification.
whyNot: It generates less growth, and at lower risk. That is the trade-off.
There is no such restriction.
Penetration is largely achieved through marketing.

questions.stem: What is the aim of portfolio analysis?
options: To judge whether the whole range of products is balanced
To decide the price of each product
To measure the profitability of the business
To choose a single product to focus on
questions.why: Cash generators funding growth products, some new bets being tested, weak products pruned. Judging each product in isolation leaves a business with either no growth or no cash.
whyNot: Pricing is a separate decision.
Profitability is measured by ratios, not by portfolio analysis.
The point is balance across the range, not concentration on one.
